lessons.title: Propositional logic and proof
lessons.prerequisite: Comfort with true/false statements and basic algebra.
lessons.intuition: A proposition has a definite truth value. Logic asks whether the structure of an argument is valid, independently of the subject matter. First translate sentences into symbols; then reason about all possible assignments, not just one convenient example.

sections.title: Connectives and implication
sections.body: AND is true only when both operands are true; OR is inclusive and false only when both are false. Negation reverses the truth value. \(P\to Q\) is equivalent to \(\neg P\lor Q\): the promise fails only when P is true and Q is false. \(P\leftrightarrow Q\) requires equal truth values. XOR requires unequal values.

sections.title: Equivalence and normal forms
sections.body: Two expressions are equivalent if their truth-table columns match for every assignment. De Morgan’s laws change ¬(\(P\land Q\)) to ¬P∨¬Q and ¬(\(P\lor Q\)) to ¬P∧¬Q. Distribute AND over OR to obtain disjunctive normal form, or OR over AND for conjunctive normal form. A tautology is always true; a contradiction is always false; a satisfiable expression is true for at least one assignment.

sections.title: Checking an argument
sections.body: An argument with premises A₁,…,Aₖ and conclusion C is valid if (A₁∧…∧Aₖ)→C is a tautology. To refute validity, find an assignment making all premises true and the conclusion false. The contrapositive \(\neg Q\to\neg P\) is equivalent to \(P\to Q\); the converse \(Q\to P\) is not generally equivalent.

sections.title: Necessary versus sufficient: translating words
sections.body: “P only if Q” means that whenever P holds, Q must hold: \(P\to Q\). “P if Q” means Q is enough to establish P: \(Q\to P\). For example, “a number is divisible by 4 only if it is even” states divisibility by 4 implies evenness; the reverse is refuted by 6. A necessary condition can hold even when the target property does not. To test a proposed equivalence, translate each direction separately and look for a counterexample. In proofs, modus ponens uses P and \(P\to Q\) to infer Q, while modus tollens uses ¬Q and \(P\to Q\) to infer ¬P. Inferring P merely from Q is the invalid pattern called affirming the consequent.

steps.title: Choose a distinguishing assignment
steps.explanation: Choose the antecedent of the first implication false and its consequent true. This is deliberately asymmetric; P=Q would not expose the difference.

steps.title: Evaluate the original implication
steps.explanation: Material implication excludes only a true antecedent with a false consequent. A false antecedent therefore makes this implication true.

steps.title: Evaluate the converse
steps.explanation: Reversing the implication changes which statement is the antecedent. Here the converse asserts that a true Q forces a false P.

steps.title: Draw the logical conclusion
steps.explanation: Equivalence requires agreement on every assignment. One disagreement is enough to refute it; no full truth table is necessary.

examples.given: P and Q can independently be true or false.
examples.goal: Decide whether an implication is equivalent to its converse.
examples.strategy: Disprove equivalence by finding one truth assignment where the two expressions disagree.
examples.answer: The implication and its converse are not equivalent.
examples.verification: The contrapositive \(\neg Q\to\neg P\) is true on this assignment, consistent with its equivalence to \(P\to Q\).

examples.prompt: Test: \(P\to Q\), \(Q\to R\), therefore \(P\to R\)

steps.title: Translate the condition
steps.explanation: A false implication requires a true antecedent and false consequent. These values are forced by the attempted counterexample.

steps.title: Calculate carefully
steps.explanation: Since P is true, the first premise can remain true only if Q is also true.

steps.title: Conclude and interpret
steps.explanation: The second premise then forces R true, contradicting the R=false requirement. No satisfying assignment to the premises falsifies the conclusion.

examples.strategy: Try to make the conclusion false while keeping both premises true.
examples.answer: \(Q\to R\) then forces R=true, a contradiction. No counterexample exists; the argument is valid.
examples.verification: This is implication chaining, also called hypothetical syllogism. The counterexample test verifies it without presuming the conclusion.

lessons.method:
A proposition is a declarative statement with a definite truth value. “7 is prime” is a proposition; “x is prime” depends on x and is a predicate; a command has no truth value. Symbols P and Q let us reason about statement structure without repeatedly discussing their subject matter. Negation reverses a truth value; conjunction requires both inputs true; disjunction requires at least one true. Mathematical OR is inclusive unless stated otherwise.
A truth table enumerates all assignments. With n independent propositions there are \(2^n\) rows, because each independently has two choices. Create columns for smaller subexpressions before the final expression. Parentheses determine grouping, so calculate inside them first. A tautology is true on every row, a contradiction false on every row, and a contingent formula true on some rows and false on others.
For GATE, “always true” requires every row, while refuting it requires just one false row. Do not confuse a proposition’s actual real-world truth with a formula’s truth under arbitrary assignments. A table is also a proof: it exhausts the finite cases rather than testing a few favorable examples. Implication \(P	o Q\) says that a true P cannot coexist with a false Q. It does not assert that P is true, or that Q can occur only because of P. Its truth-table definition is \(P	o Q\equiv
eg P\lor Q\). A false antecedent satisfies this constraint, which is why an implication can be true when its antecedent is false. “P only if Q” makes Q necessary for P; “P if Q” makes Q sufficient for P and translates as \(Q	o P\).

steps.title: Assume a failing conclusion

steps.explanation: The premise P rules out every assignment with a false antecedent.

steps.title: Test the first premise
steps.explanation: The remaining candidate violates \(P\to Q\), so no counterexample satisfies both premises.

steps.explanation: This assignment satisfies the premise Q.

steps.title: Check the implication
steps.explanation: Both premises are true while P is false, furnishing a counterexample.

examples.prompt: How many of the eight assignments satisfy (\(P\lor Q\))∧(¬P∨R)?

steps.title: Apply the first rule

steps.title: Apply the second rule

example.prompt: Prove that ¬(\(P\land Q\)) is logically equivalent to ¬P∨¬Q.
example.strategy: List the cases → Evaluate the left side → Evaluate the right side → Compare columns

steps.title: List the cases
steps.explanation: Two independent propositions give four assignments; none may be omitted.

steps.title: Evaluate the left side
steps.explanation: The conjunction is true only in the first row, and its negation reverses that column.

steps.title: Evaluate the right side
steps.explanation: Both negations are false only when P and Q are both true.

steps.title: Compare columns
steps.explanation: The final columns agree in every row, proving equivalence.

lessons.title: C types, expressions, pointers and memory
lessons.intuition: C exposes the relationship between a value and its storage. A pointer stores an address; dereferencing accesses the object there. Tracing code requires tracking types, lifetimes and sequencing, rather than assuming every expression has a predictable machine result.

sections.title: Types and evaluation
sections.body: Integer promotions and conversions affect arithmetic. Integer division truncates toward zero; floating operands change division behaviour. Logical AND and logical OR short-circuit, evaluating the right side only when necessary. sizeof measures bytes and normally does not evaluate its operand, except relevant variable-length-array cases. Do not assume int is always four bytes unless the question states the machine model.

sections.title: Pointers and arrays
sections.body: For a pointer p to T, p+1 advances by sizeof(T) bytes within a valid array range. An array expression usually decays to a pointer to its first element, but sizeof on an actual in-scope array returns full array size. Function parameters written as arrays are adjusted to pointers. Dereferencing a one-past-the-end pointer is invalid even though forming it is permitted.

sections.title: Lifetime and undefined behaviour
sections.body: Automatic local objects cease to exist after their scope exits; returning their addresses creates dangling pointers. steps.title: Integer operation

steps.title: Assignment conversion
steps.explanation: Conversion happens after that division.

steps.title: Floating operation
steps.explanation: The floating operand changes the arithmetic before division.

examples.prompt: For initialized ints x=6 and y=3, find x&y and x&&y.

steps.title: Write bit patterns
steps.explanation: The nonzero values have different sets of one bits.

steps.title: Apply bitwise AND
steps.explanation: Only the shared middle bit survives, giving two.

steps.title: Apply logical AND
steps.explanation: Both operands are true, so the logical result is exactly one.

examples.prompt: Trace int x=0,y=5; int z=(x!=0)&&(y/x>1). Does division execute?
examples.strategy: Evaluate the left operand → Use short circuit → Assign the result

steps.title: Evaluate the left operand
steps.explanation: The comparison is false because x is zero.

steps.title: Use short circuit
steps.explanation: Logical AND skips its right operand after a false left operand.

steps.title: Assign the result
steps.explanation: No division occurs, so this expression does not divide by zero.

examples.prompt: With eight-bit unsigned char and a 32-bit int, trace unsigned char u=0; u--; Is this signed overflow?
examples.strategy: Promote the operand → Compute before conversion → Store in the narrow unsigned type

steps.title: Promote the operand
steps.explanation: The arithmetic uses int because it can represent all unsigned-char values.

steps.title: Compute before conversion
steps.explanation: This int result is representable and does not overflow.

steps.title: Store in the narrow unsigned type
steps.explanation: The assignment conversion wraps to the unsigned-char range.

examples.answer: u=255; the operation is defined under the supplied widths.
examples.verification: Adding one modulo 256 returns zero, confirming the wrap; no out-of-range signed arithmetic was performed.

example.prompt: For int a[5] and sizeof(int)=4, p=&a[1]. Where does p+2 point?
example.strategy: Locate current index → Apply element scaling → Determine target

steps.title: Locate current index
steps.explanation: p refers to element one, not the beginning of the array.

steps.title: Apply element scaling
steps.explanation: Two int-sized steps are eight bytes.

steps.title: Determine target
steps.explanation: The index advances from one to three within bounds.

examples.prompt: For int a[]={10,20,30}, int *p=a,*q=p; execute *q=11; p++; *p=22. Find a and both targets.
examples.strategy: Create aliases → Move only p → Write the new target

steps.title: Create aliases
steps.explanation: Initially p and q both designate a[0]. Writing through q changes a[0] to 11.

steps.title: Move only p
steps.explanation: p++ advances p to a[1]; q still designates a[0].

steps.title: Write the new target
steps.explanation: *p=22 changes a[1], leaving a[2] unchanged.

examples.prompt: A valid int a[6] has base byte address 1000 and sizeof(int)=4. p=&a[4], q=&a[1]. Find p−q and their byte separation.
examples.strategy: Locate each address → Subtract typed pointers → Separate byte distance

steps.title: Locate each address
steps.explanation: Scale the two indices by four bytes from the same base.

steps.title: Subtract typed pointers
steps.explanation: C pointer subtraction reports element count within this array.

steps.title: Separate byte distance
steps.explanation: Byte separation is the element count multiplied by element width.

examples.verification: q+3 equals p; multiplying the typed difference by sizeof(int) reproduces the address difference.

examples.prompt: For int a[3], p=a+3. Classify forming p, comparing p==a+3, and reading *p.
examples.strategy: Form the boundary → Compare the boundary → Check dereference

steps.title: Form the boundary
steps.explanation: a+3 is the permitted one-past pointer for this array.

steps.title: Compare the boundary
steps.explanation: Equality comparison with the same one-past expression is valid and true.

steps.title: Check dereference
steps.explanation: There is no a[3] element, so *p cannot be read as an array value.

examples.answer: Formation and comparison are valid; dereferencing p has undefined behavior.

examples.prompt: For int a[2][3] at byte address 200 with four-byte ints, locate a[1][2].
examples.strategy: Count complete rows → Add the column → Scale to bytes

steps.title: Count complete rows
steps.explanation: The first index skips one entire row of three ints.

steps.title: Add the column
steps.explanation: Column two is two additional elements within the second row.

steps.title: Scale to bytes
steps.explanation: Multiply the total element offset by the int width.

examples.verification: The six element addresses are 200,204,208,212,216,220, so the target is the final element.

examples.strategy: Use the actual object → Adjust the parameter → Measure that parameter

steps.title: Use the actual object
steps.explanation: a in the caller is an array object containing seven ints.

steps.title: Adjust the parameter
steps.explanation: The array-form parameter b has type pointer to int in the function.

steps.title: Measure that parameter
steps.explanation: sizeof sees a pointer object, not the caller's full array.

examples.answer: The sizes are 28 bytes and 8 bytes.
examples.verification: Changing the caller array extent changes its object size but does not change the adjusted parameter pointer width.

examples.prompt: Given int a[2][3], is a[0][3] a valid way to read a[1][0] because rows are adjacent?
examples.strategy: Identify the inner object → Check its index → Separate layout from permission

steps.title: Identify the inner object
steps.explanation: a[0] is an array containing exactly three ints.

steps.title: Check its index
steps.explanation: Index three is one past that row and cannot be dereferenced.

steps.title: Separate layout from permission
steps.explanation: Contiguous neighboring storage does not extend the first row's indexing bounds.

steps.title: First call
steps.explanation: The object persists after return.

steps.title: Second call
steps.explanation: The next call sees the previously stored value.

steps.title: Create separate objects
steps.explanation: The block declaration creates a new automatic x while the global x remains five.

steps.title: Execute the local increment
steps.explanation: The visible name binds to the local object, so the global is untouched.

steps.title: Leave the scope
steps.explanation: The local lifetime ends and the outer binding becomes visible again.

For equal fractional rise/fall r, final multiplier is 1−r². Quantitative aptitude also rewards translating a verbal condition into a short equation before testing options. Keep exact fractions where possible, and apply rounding only at the end. A ratio a:b states relative magnitudes, not actual values. Represent two quantities as ak and bk with one common scale k. If their total is T, k=T/(a+b); if a difference is given use the difference of coefficients. Ratios can compare different units only after consistent conversion or with their dimensional meaning clearly retained.
Combine ratios through a common shared quantity: for A:B and B:C, scale both so B’s coefficients agree. Directly appending unrelated coefficients gives the wrong combined proportion. For a constant-rate worker completing one job in t time units, rate is 1/t jobs per unit time. Independent workers on the same divisible job add rates, not durations. The reciprocal of total rate gives total completion time. If efficiencies vary, work stops or workers interfere, model those changes rather than assuming the simple independent formula.
Travel uses distance=speed×time. Fractions of an income add because they share one base, whereas mixture percentages must be weighted by their different volumes. Average travel speed uses total distance divided by total elapsed time; it is not automatically an arithmetic mean of the supplied speeds. Reversing a change requires dividing by its multiplier. A ratio describes relative quantities through one shared scale, and changing one part can change the ratio without changing every component. For a fixed total, divide by the sum of ratio coefficients; for a mixture change, retain the unchanged substance and introduce an unknown for the added substance. Convert units before addition or division. A “negative worker” such as a drain subtracts rate under a constant-rate model.
Make a table of rates and active time intervals for workers joining/leaving. Accumulated work is sum of rate×duration on each interval and cannot exceed the required job before a phase change is reached. GATE aptitude options often exploit averaging times rather than rates. Check whether a combined faster rate yields a time smaller than either worker’s solo time.

depth.body: For independent constant-rate work on a divisible job, convert each completion time into jobs per unit time before combining contributions. When a participant joins later, the rate changes at that event and accumulated work from the earlier interval must be preserved. A drain or opposing activity contributes a negative rate; adding durations cannot express that cancellation. Check whether the remaining work can be completed before the next event, and whether the net rate is positive, zero or negative. The exercises assume uninterrupted constant performance, no interference and no capacity overflow effects, so each phase's rate times duration provides an exact conservation calculation.
